concepts.title: Concept of Self: Personal and Social Identity
concepts.definition: The self is the whole set of conscious ideas, thoughts and feelings a person holds about her or his own existence; it splits into a personal identity that marks one off from everybody else and a social identity that ties one to a group, and it works both as the knower (subject) and the known (object).
concepts.formula: self = personal_identity + social_identity ; subject_knower plus object_known
concepts.key_idea: A newborn has no self - it takes shape through interaction with parents, friends and teachers, and it keeps changing with experience.
concepts.textbook_ref: lepy102.txt, Concept of Self (Activity 2.1, self as subject and object, biological/personal/social self)
question_patterns: distinguish personal identity from social identity with one example of each
how does the self act as both subject and object in knowing itself?
why does a newborn child have no idea of self at birth?
explain the difference between the personal self and the familial or relational self
in Class 12 psychology, what does self as totality of conscious experience mean?
give one situation where the self expands to include others and one where it withdraws inward

solution_steps.action: check the two-directional status of self
solution_steps.explain: as subject the self does the knowing; as object it is the thing that gets observed and known
the self emerges only as the child grows and interacts with significant people, so it is modifiable rather than inborn

worked_examples.q: Which identity marks one person off from everybody else: personal or social?

concepts.title: Self-esteem, Self-efficacy and Self-regulation
concepts.definition: Self-esteem is the value judgment a person passes on her or his own worth; self-efficacy is the belief that one personally controls life outcomes rather than luck or fate; and self-regulation is the capacity to organise, monitor and restrain one's own behaviour, including delaying gratification.
concepts.formula: self_esteem = own_worth_judgment ; self_efficacy = perceived_personal_control ; self_regulation = organised_monitored_behaviour
concepts.key_idea: By age 6-7 children judge themselves in four areas - academic, social, physical-athletic and appearance - and warm, accepting parenting raises esteem while over-assisting parents lower it.
concepts.textbook_ref: lepy102.txt, sections on Self-esteem (four areas), Self-efficacy (Bandura's social learning basis), Self-regulation (observation, self-instruction, self-reinforcement)
question_patterns: define self-esteem and name the four areas in which children judge themselves by age six or seven
how does Bandura's social learning theory explain the growth of self-efficacy?
which three psychological techniques help in developing self-control - describe each briefly
why do children whose parents decide everything for them often develop low self-esteem?
what is meant by delay or deferment of gratification, and why does it matter for long-term goals?
contrast a person high on self-efficacy with one who attributes outcomes to luck or fate

solution_steps.explain: academic competence, social competence, physical or athletic competence, and physical appearance are the areas established by 6-7 years
observation of one's own behaviour, self-instruction, and self-reinforcement are the three psychological techniques of self-control

worked_examples.q: The value judgment a person passes on her own worth is called what?

concepts.title: Culture and Self: Indian versus Western Views
concepts.definition: Western culture draws a comparatively fixed line between self and others, keeping individual and group as separate entities, whereas the Indian view lets that line shift - the self sometimes fuses with the cosmos or the group and at other times turns wholly inward.
concepts.key_idea: Individualistic Western cultures hold self and group apart, while collectivistic Asian cultures keep the self in harmonious co-existence with its group.
concepts.textbook_ref: lepy102.txt, Culture and Self (Figure 2.1 self and group boundaries in Western and Indian perspectives)
question_patterns: how does the Indian notion of self differ from the Western notion?
why are many Western cultures called individualistic and Asian cultures collectivistic?
explain the shifting boundary between self and other in the Indian cultural view
what dichotomies does Western thinking draw between self and other, and man and nature?
in the Indian view what happens to the self-boundary from one moment to the next?

solution_steps.explain: the Western boundary between self and other stays relatively fixed, while the Indian boundary shifts between fusion and withdrawal
in the Indian view the self is not separated from its own group - both co-exist harmoniously - whereas Western culture keeps them at a distance

worked_examples.q: Which culture keeps a comparatively fixed boundary between self and others: Western or Indian?

concepts.title: Type and Trait Approaches to Personality
concepts.definition: Type approaches sort people into broad behavioural patterns - Hippocrates' four humours, Charak Samhita's tridosha and trigunas, Sheldon's body builds, Jung's introvert-extravert, and Friedman and Rosenman's Type-A and Type-B - while trait approaches such as Allport's cardinal-central-secondary scheme, Cattell's sixteen source traits and Eysenck's dimensions rate people on specific attributes along which they differ consistently.
concepts.key_idea: Types are simple and stereotype-prone; traits are relatively stable over time, fairly consistent across situations, and their combinations create individual differences.
concepts.textbook_ref: lepy102.txt, Type Approaches and Trait Approaches (Sheldon, Jung, Type-A/B/C/D; Allport, Cattell's 16PF, Eysenck, Box 2.2 Big Five)
question_patterns: how does the trait approach to personality differ from the type approach?
name the four humoural types proposed by Hippocrates and the three doshas of Charak Samhita
describe the three body-build types in Sheldon's typology with their temperaments
why are people with Type-A personality more prone to hypertension and coronary heart disease?
list Allport's cardinal, central and secondary traits with one example of each
state the two dimensions of Eysenck's theory and the third dimension added later
name the five factors of the Big Five model of personality with one feature of each

solution_steps.action: check the classification logic of types
solution_steps.explain: each behavioural pattern defines one type and people are placed by similarity; the fit is usually too neat to be true, which is the standard criticism

solution_steps.action: check the three stability claims for traits
solution_steps.explain: traits stay relatively stable over time, remain generally consistent across situations, and vary in strength and combination between individuals

worked_examples.q: Sorting people into broad behavioural patterns is which approach: type or trait?

concepts.title: Freud: Structure of Personality and Defence Mechanisms
concepts.definition: Freud pictures the mind as three levels of consciousness - conscious, preconscious and unconscious - and personality as a contest among id (pleasure principle), ego (reality principle) and superego (moral branch); when the ego cannot bear anxiety it distorts reality through defence mechanisms such as repression, projection, denial, reaction formation and rationalisation.
concepts.formula: personality_structure = id_pleasure + ego_reality + superego_moral ; defence = anxiety_reduced_by_distorting_reality
concepts.key_idea: The libido energises the id; unresolved conflict shows up in slips, jokes and dreams, and only extreme use of defences produces maladjustment.
concepts.textbook_ref: lepy102.txt, Psychodynamic Approach (levels of consciousness, id-ego-superego, ego defence mechanisms, free association and dream analysis)
question_patterns: how does Freud explain the structure of personality through id, ego and superego?
differentiate the pleasure principle of the id from the reality principle of the ego with an example
define a defence mechanism and name four major ones described by Freud
why is repression called the most important defence mechanism?
a student buys new pens after failing an exam and says they will improve her marks - which defence mechanism is at work?
what are the three levels of consciousness in Freud's model of the mind?
which instinctual force energises the id according to Freud?

solution_steps.explain: id demands immediate gratification, ego gratifies needs realistically, and superego judges whether gratification is ethical by internalising parental authority
a defence reduces anxiety by distorting reality; it is normal in moderation but becomes maladjustment when reality is truly distorted

worked_examples.q: Which Freudian structure obeys the pleasure principle?

concepts.title: Psychosexual Stages and Post-Freudian Theories
concepts.section: Stages of Personality Development / Post-Freudian Approaches
concepts.definition: Freud places personality growth in five psychosexual stages - oral, anal, phallic, latency and genital - where failure at any stage fixes development there or pushes it back; post-Freudians widened the account: Jung's collective unconscious of archetypes, Horney's basic anxiety from disturbed childhood relations, Adler's inferiority complex and individual psychology, Fromm's social orientation, and Erikson's lifelong search for ego identity.
concepts.formula: stages = oral + anal + phallic + latency + genital ; fixation_or_regression = unresolved_stage_conflict
concepts.key_idea: The Oedipus complex is resolved in the phallic stage by identifying with the same-sex parent; neo-analytic theorists trimmed sexuality and enlarged the ego and social forces.
concepts.textbook_ref: lepy102.txt, five psychosexual stages with Oedipus and Electra complexes; Post-Freudian Approaches (Jung, Horney, Adler, Fromm, Erikson) and their criticisms
question_patterns: name Freud's five psychosexual stages in order with the pleasure focus of each
what is fixation and how does regression return a person to an earlier stage?
explain the resolution of the Oedipus complex in the phallic stage
how does Jung's collective unconscious with its archetypes differ from Freud's unconscious?
how would Horney's account of a disorder differ from Adler's inferiority-based explanation?
which post-Freudian theorist made the adolescent identity crisis central to development?
state two criticisms levelled against psychodynamic theories

solution_steps.action: check the stage sequence and its failure modes
solution_steps.explain: development moves from oral to anal, phallic, latency and genital; failure arrests growth at a stage (fixation) or drives the person back to a less mature one (regression)
neo-analytic theories downplay id sexuality and aggression, expand the ego, and stress creativity, competence and problem solving

worked_examples.q: How many psychosexual stages did Freud propose?

concepts.title: Humanistic, Behavioural and Cultural Approaches
concepts.section: Behavioural Approach / Cultural Approach / Humanistic Approach
concepts.definition: Behaviourists treat personality as reinforced stimulus-response learning where the response is the structural unit; the cultural approach reads personality as adaptation to a group's economic maintenance system, as the Birhor hunting-gathering and agricultural contrasts show; and humanists - Rogers with the real and ideal self plus unconditional positive regard, Maslow with self-actualisation at the top of the needs hierarchy - see people striving to fulfil their potential.
concepts.formula: rogers_congruence = real_self matches ideal_self -> fully_functioning_person ; maslow_top_need = self_actualisation
concepts.key_idea: A gap between real and ideal self breeds unhappiness; children of hunting-gathering societies learn independence and achievement while agricultural socialisation rewards obedience and nurturance.
concepts.textbook_ref: lepy102.txt, Behavioural Approach (response as structural unit), Cultural Approach (Birhor example), Humanistic Approach (Rogers fully functioning person, Maslow self-actualisation, Box 2.3 healthy person)
question_patterns: what is the main proposition of the humanistic approach and what did Maslow mean by self-actualisation?
why does a discrepancy between real self and ideal self produce dissatisfaction in Rogers' view?
which condition did Rogers name as necessary for enhancing a person's self-concept?
how does the behavioural approach treat the response as the structural unit of personality?
compare the personality qualities socialised in hunting-gathering and agricultural societies
using Carl Rogers' terms, describe a family that disapproves of a child's career choice while claiming to love him
what role does the economic maintenance system play in the cultural approach?

solution_steps.explain: correspondence between real and ideal self brings happiness, while discrepancy breeds unhappiness and dissatisfaction
personality qualities track the demands of a group's livelihood - independence and achievement orientation suit hunting-gathering, obedience and responsibility suit agriculture

worked_examples.q: Which need crowns Maslow's hierarchy: self-actualisation or safety?

concepts.title: Self-Report Measures and Rating-Scale Scoring
concepts.definition: Self-report measures are structured questionnaires - MMPI with 567 true-false statements on 10 subscales, Eysenck's EPQ, Cattell's 16PF - where responses are scored quantitatively and read against norms; their weak points are social desirability and acquiescence, the habit of agreeing with items regardless of content.
concepts.key_idea: Average the ratings a person gives across areas to quantify a self-report score; high numbers on endorsed statements mean high standing on that attribute.
concepts.textbook_ref: lepy102.txt, Self-report Measures (MMPI and MMPI-2 with 567 statements and 10 subscales, JMPI, EPQ, 16PF, social desirability and acquiescence biases)
question_patterns: a child rates her academic, social, physical and appearance areas - find her mean self-esteem score

which Indian inventory was modelled on the MMPI?

why do responses on a rating scale get accepted at face value in self-report measures?
compute the average rating from a four-area self-esteem checklist with given marks

solution_steps.action: add the ratings across the four self-esteem areas
solution_steps.explain: each area - academic, social, physical-athletic and appearance - carries one rating on the scale

solution_steps.action: divide the summed ratings by the number of areas
solution_steps.explain: the mean puts all respondents on one comparable scale regardless of how many items were used

worked_examples.q: How many true-false statements does the MMPI carry?

concepts.title: Projective Techniques: Rorschach and TAT
concepts.definition: Projective techniques reach unconscious motives through unstructured stimuli on which people project feelings and needs; shared features include ambiguous material, hidden purpose, no right or wrong answers, and subjective lengthy scoring; the Rorschach inkblot test, Thematic Apperception Test, Rosenzweig picture-frustration study, sentence completion and draw-a-person tests are the standard examples.
concepts.key_idea: The Rorschach set holds ten symmetric blots - five black and white, two with red ink, three pastel - administered in a performance proper phase and an inquiry phase.
concepts.textbook_ref: lepy102.txt, Projective Techniques (five shared features, Rorschach 10 inkblots, TAT 30 picture cards plus one blank card by Morgan and Murray)
question_patterns: how many inkblots make up the Rorschach test and what is their colour composition?

in the Rosenzweig picture-frustration study, on what are responses analysed?

solution_steps.action: combine the achromatic cards with the red-inked cards
solution_steps.explain: five blots are printed in black and white and two carry red ink

solution_steps.action: add the pastel-coloured blots to reach the full set
solution_steps.explain: the remaining three blots use pastel colours, completing the standard ten-card series

worked_examples.q: How many symmetric inkblots does the Rorschach test hold?

worked_examples.problem: On a four-area self-esteem checklist, a child rates academic competence 4, social competence 5, physical-athletic competence 3 and physical appearance 4 on a five-point scale. Find her mean self-esteem score.

steps.action: divide by the number of areas

worked_examples.answer: esteem_mean = 4, a generally positive self-view across the four areas assessed by age 6-7

worked_examples.problem: Verify the composition of the Rorschach inkblot series: 5 blots in black and white, 2 carrying red ink, and 3 in pastel colours. How many cards does the full set contain?

steps.action: add the black-and-white and red-ink cards
add the pastel cards to complete the series

worked_examples.answer: blot_total = 10, the standard Rorschach series administered in performance proper and inquiry phases
